name: Pale Olivine
lede: Pale Olivine is a soft, pale yellow-green named for olivine, the gem-grade mineral better known in its greener, deeper form as peridot.

sections.title: A lighter cut of the mineral
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color book places this value on plate XXXII, hue 35″, tone f [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 groups a cluster of related names under block 121, including Chartreuse Tint, Oyster Grey and Succory, a sign the 1912 plates drew several close pale yellow-greens into one dictionary block [1]. [[gem:peridot|Peridot]], the gem cut from olivine, usually runs darker and more saturated than this pale swatch [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[oural-green]] and [[pale-sage]], at Compare [[sage|Sage]], [[ash|Ash]] and [[moss|Moss]], the names our archive finds sharing its canvases most [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a color within six units of this one in 361, about 1.5 percent, as photographed [2]. It is unusually common in British painting, 39 of 593 United Kingdom works, over four times the archive's rate, and Joseph Mallord William Turner carries it in 3 of his 14 dated works [2]. The earliest match is Piero della Francesca's 1470 diptych of Federico da Montefeltro and Battista Sforza, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. The match is a screen-color comparison on aged, varnished paintings, not a mineral test [2].

surprises: United Kingdom: 39 of 593 works carry it, 4.33x the archive rate

questions.q: What gem is cut from olivine?
True or false: Pale Olivine turns up far more often in British paintings than in the archive overall.

openers: A gem mineral's name, but much paler than the peridot it's cut into.
